items.title: Hidden Pod Startup Latency: Container Image Pull - Omer Oz, LinkedIn
items.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
items.content:
<article>Connect with the cloud native community and explore CNCF events: https://kubecon.io

Hidden Pod Startup Latency: Container Image Pull - Omer Oz, LinkedIn

Pod startup latency directly impacts service responsiveness, autoscaling speed, and incident recovery on Kubernetes. Yet much of that latency is dominated by the image pull step; which is mostly hidden.

Drawing on a real LinkedIn production case study — over 500K bare-metal hosts, 25M cores, and pod density averaging beyond 50 per host in our densest clusters — we’ll show how we cut the long tail of pod startup latency by 72% through reducing image pull latency by 72% at P99 and 75% at P50. We'll examine how container image pulls contribute to startup latency: taking a deep dive into the image pull path to identify bottlenecks and build a mental model, then covering the practical levers we have — compression, kubelet and containerd configuration, and P2P caching.</article>

items.title: Containerd: Project Update and Deep Dive - Wei Fu, Microsoft & Samuel Karp, Google
items.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
items.content:
<article>Connect with the cloud native community and explore CNCF events: https://kubecon.io

Containerd: Project Update and Deep Dive - Wei Fu, Microsoft & Samuel Karp, Google

Join containerd maintainers for project update and deep dive into the latest updates on containerd.  LLM-assisted vulnerability discovery has had a big impact on containerd: we'll discuss the impact on the project and changes we've made to improve our security response.  For Kubernetes users, we will cover how the new containerd release cycle, support window, and upgrade safety changes make feature availability faster and make long-term support available across Kubernetes versions.  We’ll then dive into the exciting work going on in the containerd ecosystem, including further developments in the Node Resource Interface (NRI) and EROFS snapshotter.</article>

items.title: CoHDI: Bridging Kubernetes and Disaggregated Memory for Memory... Naoki Oguchi & Hidetsugu Sugiyama
items.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
items.content:
<article>Connect with the cloud native community and explore CNCF events: https://kubecon.io

CoHDI: Bridging Kubernetes and Disaggregated Memory for Memory-Aware LLM Inference - Naoki Oguchi, Fsas Technologies Inc. & Hidetsugu Sugiyama, Red Hat

LLM inference is becoming memory-centric, where capacity, bandwidth, and data movement dominate performance and cost. Techniques such as continuous batching and prefill/decode disaggregation (e.g., vLLM, LLM-d) improve efficiency within a node, but introduce a new challenge: managing large-scale KV cache across distributed nodes.
At the same time, disaggregated memory technologies like CXL enable memory to scale beyond node boundaries, creating an opportunity to extend Kubernetes with memory-aware orchestration while preserving its model.
We present CoHDI, a CNCF sandbox project that bridges Kubernetes and disaggregated infrastructure. CoHDI provides abstractions for memory-aware resource management across GPU HBM, DRAM, and CXL, and acts as a mediation layer with runtimes like vLLM to enable coordinated placement of compute and KV cache.
Using a vLLM prototype, we demonstrate early results showing the impact of tiered KV placement on concurrency, latency, and GPU utilization.</article>

items.title: When in-toto Met OPA: Turning Attestations into E2E Security &... Snahil Singh & Trishank Kuppusamy
items.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
items.content:
<article>Connect with the cloud native community and explore CNCF events: https://kubecon.io

When in-toto Met OPA: Turning Attestations into E2E Security & Compliance with Cloud Native Policies - Snahil Singh & Trishank Kuppusamy, Apple

Today, there are in-toto attestations about artifacts like code reviews & build provenance, but no policies to turn them into end-to-end software supply chain security narratives. Was the same container image uploaded to the registry as the one built on CI? Did the CI use two-party-reviewed source code?

The in-toto policy framework was designed to connect different attestations together. It allows different policy languages with reproducible, portable verification, but no compliant implementation existed for a de facto engine. OPA is such an engine, but was missing a supply chain security story.

We present the first implementation of the in-toto policy framework written on OPA enabling ergonomic, reusable, and extensible policies powerful enough to verify artifacts from development to deployment. Results are reproducible & portable so different engines can verify them despite using different languages. We illustrate with examples ranging from container registries to package managers.</article>

items.title: Life After Strimzi 1.0.0 - Jakub Scholz, Cloudera
items.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
items.content:
<article>Connect with the cloud native community and explore CNCF events: https://kubecon.io

Life After Strimzi 1.0.0 - Jakub Scholz, Cloudera

Earlier this year, Strimzi celebrated its 1.0.0 release - a major project milestone. After briefly recalling the 1.0.0 release and its main changes, this talk will focus on our roadmap and on where the project is heading next. Gateway API support opens new ways to connect to your Apache Kafka clusters. A new pluggability mechanism inspired by Kubernetes Admission Controllers and policy engines such as Kyverno or Open Policy Agent makes it easier to customize and extend Strimzi. And more flexible security configuration gives you finer control over how your Apache Kafka cluster is secured. Those are just some of the features that are planned or already in progress. We will cover them in this talk and show you how to get involved and help shape them. You will leave this session with a clear picture of the future of Strimzi.</article>

items.title: CNCF CTO Chris Aniszczyk on New Kubernetes AI Certifications
items.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
items.content:
<article>At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America, CNCF CTO Chris Aniszczyk shared how we are expanding our certification roadmap to match the rapid growth of AI workloads on Kubernetes.

Following the rapid adoption of our AI conformance program, CNCF is collaborating with Linux Foundation Education and the open source community to develop two new vendor-neutral credentials planned for 2027. The Kubernetes AI Associate will introduce foundational AI terms such as prefill and decode, while the Certified Kubernetes Inference Engineer will validate practical expertise in running and scaling inference workloads on Kubernetes.

These upcoming credentials expand a portfolio that includes our newly launched Certified Kubernetes Network Engineer certification, helping engineers build verified skills across modern cloud native infrastructure.

Learn more about CNCF certifications and how you can help develop the new AI exams: https://www.cncf.io/announcements/2026/11/10/cncf-launches-certified-kubernetes-network-engineer-certification-ckne-to-advance-production-ready-networking-skills-for-ai-era/

#CNCF #CloudNative #Kubernetes #AI #KubeCon</article>

items.title: Stop Templating YAML: Build Configuration Supply Chains with kpt and Porch - Liam Fallon
items.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
items.content:
<article>Connect with the cloud native community and explore CNCF events: https://kubecon.io

Stop Templating YAML: Build Configuration Supply Chains with kpt and Porch - Liam Fallon

Kubernetes made infrastructure declarative, yet teams still manage configuration through templates, overlays, Git conventions, and custom automation. At scale, this creates YAML sprawl, inconsistent validation, and fragile workflows.

This lightning talk introduces kpt, a CNCF Sandbox project that treats Kubernetes Resource Model objects as data: structured, versioned packages transformed and validated by reusable functions. Unlike template-centric approaches, kpt keeps configuration readable while separating the data from the code that operates on it.

A compact demonstration will show Porch, kpt’s package orchestration component, managing a configuration package through Kubernetes APIs from draft to approval and Git publication. Porch replaces repository-specific scripting with a consistent, automatable package lifecycle.

Attendees will learn where kpt and Porch fit in GitOps and platform engineering, and how configuration packages improve reuse, governance, and multi-cluster delivery.</article>

items.title: Your Routes, My Rules: Making Gateway API Work at Enterprise Scale - David Jumani, Solo.io
items.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
items.content:
<article>Connect with the cloud native community and explore CNCF events: https://kubecon.io

Your Routes, My Rules: Making Gateway API Work at Enterprise Scale - David Jumani, Solo.io

At enterprise scale, the hard part of running a gateway isn't the traffic, it's the people: dozens of teams who all need to ship routes without waiting on the platform team or breaking each other.
In five minutes, see how kgateway makes Gateway API work for big organizations. App teams own their routes through delegation. Platform teams keep the rules with inherited policies, and strict validation checks config with Envoy itself before it ships, so one team's mistake stays on its own route. Then a quick look under the hood: a control plane built on Istio's KRT, where kgateway and Istio make each other faster, so it scales with the org chart, and routes that reach beyond the cluster to the cloud and the mesh.</article>

items.title: KAI Scheduler: What's New & What's Next in AI Workload Orchestration - Omri Cohen, NVIDIA
items.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
items.content:
<article>Connect with the cloud native community and explore CNCF events: https://kubecon.io

KAI Scheduler: What's New & What's Next in AI Workload Orchestration - Omri Cohen, NVIDIA

As multi-tenant AI clusters grow, the KAI Scheduler continues to evolve to tackle modern k8s AI clusters challenges. In this talk, we will highlight the newest features and capabilities recently added to KAI. We will showcase how KAI enhances performance and fairness with introducing some of our latest developments including:


- GPU fractioning & virtualization: Integrating HAMI & GPU fraction support in KAI
- Multi-hierarchical gang scheduling
- Semi-preemptible burstable workloads
- Multi-hierarchical topology support
- Queue prioritization models: quota, weight, and priority
- Time-based fairness: Eliminating long-term job starvation across competing teams

Attendees will get a tour of KAI’s latest developments, real-world efficiency impacts, and a preview of what’s next on the project roadmap.</article>

items.title: Architecture Without Gatekeepers: Decoupling for Neutrality - Kate Obiidykhata, Percona
items.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
items.content:
<article>Connect with the cloud native community and explore CNCF events: https://kubecon.io

Architecture Without Gatekeepers: Decoupling for Neutrality - Kate Obiidykhata, Percona

Open source only works if the community can contribute without hitting a wall. We realized our architecture at OpenEverest was unintentionally biased toward specific tools, so we rebuilt it. I’ll share how we moved to a modular plugin system that decouples our core from specific operators. By supporting everything from Valkey to competing Postgres flavors, we’ve eliminated vendor lock-in and ensured the community—not the architecture—dictates the project's future.</article>

items.title: Velero: Faster Backups, Consistent Snapshots, Incremental... Shubham Dilip Pampattiwar, Red Hat
items.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
items.content:
<article>Connect with the cloud native community and explore CNCF events: https://kubecon.io

Velero: Faster Backups, Consistent Snapshots, Incremental Everything - Shubham Dilip Pampattiwar, Red Hat

A Velero user told us their backup window was longer than the time between backups. Their database spanned four PVCs, each snapshotted independently, and every backup copied the entire volume. Something had to change.

Velero 1.18 fixed the first two problems. Concurrent backups eliminated the single-backup queue, letting teams run in parallel. VolumeGroupSnapshots capture all database PVCs in a single crash-consistent snapshot, no more hoping volumes line up.

Velero 1.19 fixed the third. The Block Data Mover uses Change Block Tracking to back up only blocks that changed. That 500GB volume with 5GB of daily writes? It's a 5GB backup now.

Along the way, Velero joined the CNCF Sandbox, a milestone for the community and a signal that Kubernetes-native data protection is here to stay. This lightning talk covers all three and shows what's ahead.</article>

items.title: Cedar Authorization with Incomplete Information - John Kastner, AWS
items.author: CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation]
items.content:
<article>Connect with the cloud native community and explore CNCF events: https://kubecon.io

Cedar Authorization with Incomplete Information - John Kastner, AWS

Authorization decisions often depend on information that isn't easily available when you need to make a decision. In Kubernetes, for example, the API server must authorize a request before the body is decoded. Without access to all the fields, authorizers have to first over-grant permissions before using separate admission plugins to enforce fine-grained restrictions after the fact.

Cedar's partial evaluation addresses this by evaluating policies against incomplete information. When it lacks what it needs to return ""allow"" or ""deny,"" it instead produces a residual policy encoding the information needed to reach a concrete decision. Recent extensions to Cedar's partial evaluation support more fine-grained partial inputs, making this practical for real-world use. In this talk, we'll walk through Cedar policy evaluation when key attributes are unknown, producing a residual that is refined incrementally as information becomes available.</article>
